frames.subtitle: The stovetop pot behind so many Italian mornings.

frames.title: What a moka is
frames.body: A stovetop pot in three parts. Water goes in the bottom chamber, ground coffee in the basket, and steam pressure pushes the coffee up into the top chamber.

frames.title: Brew it in five moves
steps: Water in the bottom, just below the valve.
Medium-ground coffee in the basket. Don't press it.
Level it, wipe the rim, screw it shut.
Low heat, lid open so you can watch.
Off the heat as soon as it gurgles.

frames.body: Rinse it with hot water, and check your pot's manual before using soap or the dishwasher.

frames.title: Small, strong, fast
frames.body: Espresso is made by pushing hot water through finely ground coffee under pressure. A shot takes less than half a minute and fits in a tiny cup.
The brewing pressure in the Italian Espresso Institute's definition, give or take 1 bar.

frames.title: If you upgrade one thing
frames.body: Make it the grinder. Espresso needs a fine, even grind, and that is the hardest job for a cheap grinder.
Skip the gadgets until the basics taste right.

frames.title: Your questions, answered
frames.subtitle: Anything about the moka pot and home espresso.

frames.question: Why does my moka coffee taste bitter or burnt?
frames.answer: Usually the heat is too high, or the pot stays on too long. Use low heat and take it off as soon as it starts to gurgle.

frames.question: Is moka coffee the same as espresso?
frames.answer: No. A moka brews at much lower pressure, so the coffee is strong but lighter in body, with little or no crema (the golden foam on top).

frames.question: Do I need an expensive machine for good espresso?
frames.answer: Not to start. An even grind and fresh coffee change the cup more than the price of the machine.
